summary: On Postgres the schema a process declares is the database's (_delta_collections), not its own
detail: Two versions on one Postgres share _delta_collections, written by the last generateSql applied: during expand step 2 the old version's documents show the new version's columns, and a rollback's generateSql hides them from the new one. SQLite keeps each process's own schema. The cost: the expand/contract rule holds on Postgres only as 'the newest start declares'. A fix passes the listener its own schema (docTypeFromDef with the columns) and filters with it.
note: reference/migrations.md says so; tests/schema-contract.test.ts asserts invisibility on SQLite only

summary: The migration fence covers the whole database's ledger, not the migrating app's
detail: A migration sets undoable = false on every delta_ledger / _delta_ledger entry, so on a database several apps share, one app's upgrade ends every app's undo history. Ledger entries name a document, not an app; fencing by the app's document prefixes needs its docs passed to migrate. The cost: lost undo across an upgrade for apps that did not change.

summary: The JSON file has no migrations
detail: migrate runs SQL; the JSON file's rows are JSON by collection, loaded into SQLite in memory. A rename or drop there is by hand, or by moving to SQLite (exportTables / importTables) first.

summary: A Postgres whose tables init_db/ made at first boot looks lived-in to migrate
detail: With init_db's 003-tables.sql the app's tables are there before migrate's first start, so migrate runs the app's whole list against tables already at their end, and the first fails. The workaround: make the tables at start-up (applySql), vendor only the framework. A fix: `delta sql` writes the delta_migrations rows of the list beside the tables, or migrate takes { baseline: true }.

summary: Undoing a remove puts a row back with an undeclared column at its default
detail: An inverse holds the declared columns only (the schema is the contract), so an old version's undo of its own remove re-adds the row with a later version's column at its database default; the value it held is in the row's temporal history (and gone for a plain table). Postgres and SQLite alike.
